kind: decision
title: Long decisions use a summary/detail split; every refusal stays visible with its grounds
state: accepted
created: "2026-07-30T22:00:00Z"
tags: [design, information-architecture]
edges:
  - type: derives_from
    to: int-0001
    note: reasoning nobody can find is reasoning that did not survive the session
alternatives:
  - option: Let it run — no truncation, trust the measure ceilings
    why_not: >
      Honest to the record and it never hides reasoning, but a 20-alternative decision
      measured 5,316px, about 6.9 screens, for one entry. On the surface a stranger lands
      on, that is a scroll nobody finishes, and reasoning nobody reaches is not
      meaningfully published.
    revisit_if: a reader study shows people do scroll it
  - option: Progressive disclosure — show the first N, hide the rest behind details
    why_not: >
      Halves the page, but it hides the thing that makes the page persuasive. A reviewer
      testing this design as a stranger said the struck-through refusal with its
      reasoning still attached was the only element that made them want the tool. Putting
      most of them behind a click optimises the page against its own strongest device.
source:
  hook: manual

Every alternative stays visible, struck through, **with a one-line ground beneath it**.
Full reasoning expands per item via `<details>`/`<summary>` — no JavaScript, the same
collapse mechanism the chain adopted.

The distinction that matters, and the reason this beat progressive disclosure: the
summary line carries **the grounds, not just the title**. A reader scans all twenty
refusals *and why each lost* without a single click. Expansion is for the full argument,
not for the fact that an argument exists.

Chosen from rendered alternatives rather than argued in the abstract. Measured page
heights: 6.9 screens untreated, 3.7 progressive, 3.8 for this. The near-tie between the
last two is why the deciding factor was which device survived, not which was shortest.

The chain collapses in the same idiom — `… 16 further refusals on record` — so the
instrument half and the prose half now use one disclosure grammar instead of two.
